Dēn is listed among the divine helpers cooperating with Spandārmad.
Spənta Ārmaiti is named as Daena’s mother.
Daena manifests and leads onward while Sraoša guards and guides the dead.
Srōš guides Wīrāz while his own religion and deeds appear as Daena.
Sraosha escorts the soul when it encounters its personified Daēnā.

relations.myth: Righteous soul enters the divine assembly
relations.note: After Daena assists the crossing, the righteous advance toward Vohu Manah’s throne or domain.
Wahman escorts Wīrāz onward after the bridge episode involving his Daena.
Vohu Manah and Daēnā appear in adjoining stages of the soul’s journey.
The daevas and their devotees belong to Druj’s party and later to the same demonic host.
They overcome daēvic oppression and restore movement to stars, moon, and sun.
Praise and consumption of Haoma strike down or repel the daēvas.
The dēw Tārič is systematically arranged as Hordād’s opposing counterpart.
Calling upon Haurvatat’s name is said to destroy or repel innumerable daevas.
Hvar’s rising and worship prevent the daēvas from destroying the seven regions.
Mithra smashes the heads of daēvas and destroys their defiant forces.
Nāŋhais or Tarōmat is arranged as Spandarmad’s opposing demonic counterpart.

relations.myth: Cosmic opposition of the two hosts
relations.note: Later doctrine arrays Angra Mainyu and the daēvas against Spenta Mainyu and good creation.

relations.myth: Opposition of good and destructive creation
relations.note: The Daēvas belong collectively to the destructive side opposed by Spenta Mainyu.
Sraoša strikes the daēva Aēšma at night while protecting ritual and settlements.
The hostile demon Apaōša battles the rain-star Tištrya.
The dēw Akōman is systematically arranged as Wahman’s opposing counterpart.
The daēvas reject Good Mind by choosing the worst mind and destructive action.
Akəm Manah and other hostile beings oppose Vohu Manah in the struggle for Glory.
A male demon and female parīg deceive Jam and Jamag into cross-marriages.
Yima rules the demons and deprives them of prosperity.
One later account says demons cut Jam apart.
Demons labor for Jamshid, build and carry his jeweled throne.
Later tradition says Jam recovers wisdom and crafts from demons.
Cattle driven toward Druj’s den appeal to Mithra, protector of covenant and pasture.
Druj specializes as corpse pollution called Druj Nasu; later tradition sometimes distinguishes Nas as a demon.
Saoshyant stands against and overcomes the Lie and its human and demonic brood.
The future savior overcomes Druj among humanity during the final renovation.
Spenta Mainyu belongs to the truthful order structurally opposed to Druj, without a separate encounter.
Sraosha and truthful prayer repel Druj and protect against later funerary demonic danger.
Those choosing Druj depart from Vohu Manah, though no separate narrative duel is attested.
The fravashi of primordial Gayōmard is invoked within the sacred-history catalogue.
The collective Fravašis assist Hordād in the cosmic ordering of waters.

relations.myth: Regulation of the Moon’s celestial course
relations.note: The fravašis establish or sustain Māh’s course until the final renovation.
The guardian spirits escort Mithra during his progress.
Mithra is explicitly said to possess a fravashi.
Rashnu is explicitly said to possess a fravashi.
The righteous fravašis guard Zarathustra’s seed and the future salvific birth.
The future Saoshyant’s fravashi is invoked within the hymn’s sacred-history catalogue.
The Fravashis stand firm and preserve Spenta Mainyu’s good creation.
They protect worshippers with assistance from Sraosha and Ahura Mazda.
Sraosha is explicitly said to possess a fravashi.

relations.myth: Distribution of rain among the lands
relations.note: The righteous Fravašis assist the distribution of waters produced through Tishtrya's work.
Vohu Manah joins their resistance to evil in an obscure, disputed sequence.

relations.myth: Nasu enters Gayōmard’s corpse after death
relations.note: Nasu enters primordial Gayōmard from his left little toe and moves upward.
Some later accounts begin Saoshyant’s bodily resurrection with the primordial man Gayōmard.

relations.myth: Beginning and end of human history
relations.note: Gayomart begins human sacred history and the victorious Saošyant completes it.
Gayomart rises first or among the first and participates in Saošyant's final Renovation.
The Dēnkard calls earth-Spandārmad Gayōmard’s mother.
The Dēnkard polemically formulates Gayōmard as Spandārmad’s sexual partner despite also calling him her son.
Spandārmad participates as Earth in Ohrmazd's creation of Gayomart.
Earth receives one portion of Gayomart's seed after his death.

relations.myth: Death of Gayōmard and birth of humanity
relations.note: Spandārmad-earth receives one portion of Gayōmard’s purified seed.
Hōm joins Haurvatat’s water-and-immortality complex at renovation without a personal meeting.
Haoma and milk are presented in the ritual worship of Hvar.
Māh and Haoma are grouped as Vohu Manah's animal-protecting fellow-workers.
Mithra's hymn presents Haoma as the swiftly sacrificing divine priest.
Haoma says future saoshyants will praise him and asks Zarathustra to do likewise.
Haoma offers sacrifice to Sraosha on Mount Harā.
Clouds raised through Tishtrya's work travel along paths previously traversed by Haoma.
The worshipper offers victorious Haoma within Vərəθraγna's hymn for protection and battlefield victory.
Haoma's medicines share Vohu Manah's healing and animal-protecting sphere.
Wahman carries sacred hōm contributing to Zarathustra’s corporeal formation.
Haoma tells Zarathustra that his pressing rewarded Vīuuaŋᵛhant with Yima’s birth.
Haurvatāt is named jointly with enduring dominion and the other divine powers.
Haurvatāt shares collectively in the Aməša Spəṇtas' possession of Khvarenah.
Invocation of Haurvatat’s name destroys or repels Nasu and related contaminating beings.

relations.myth: Release from pollution and hostile beings
relations.note: Rashnu follows Haurvatat’s invocation and joins male yazatas in freeing the worshipper from pollution.
Haurvatāt participates in the final rite and defeats hunger.
Spandarmad, Hordād, and Amurdād form the feminine triad seated on Ohrmazd’s left.
Haurvatāt and Ārmaiti appear together as members of the beneficent heptad.
Wholeness or Perfection is bestowed through the beneficent spirit’s action.
Ahura Mazda grants Haurvatat and Amərətāt through Spəṇta Mainyu.

relations.myth: Liturgical protection with the Amesha Spentas
relations.note: Sraosha appears with Haurvatat’s divine group in protective liturgy; no separate episode survives.
Tīštrya assists Hordād in the cosmic economy of rain and waters.

relations.myth: Divine gifts obtained through good thought
relations.note: Vohu Manah and Haurvatat appear together within Ahura Mazda’s divine complex.
Haurvatāt and Vohu Manah appear jointly within the beneficent divine order.

relations.myth: Best companionship of Moon and Sun
relations.note: The hymn praises Moon and Sun as forming the best companionship.
Sun and Moon jointly command the movable heavenly bodies.
Strabo reports that Persians call the Sun Mithra.
Mithra rises over Mount Harā before the swift-horsed immortal Sun.
Mithra is invoked immediately before praise of Moon and Sun companionship.
Later practice conventionally pairs the Xwaršēd and Mihr Niyāyišns.
Hvar’s rising purifies the creations belonging to Spənta Mainyu.
Tištrya and Hvar serve among the heavenly commanders defending creation.
Hvar, Moon, Tištrya, stars, and Mithra appear together in liturgical catalogues.
Mihr cooperates with Šahrewar’s metal and its protective weapons.
A metallic fitting on Mithra’s chariot is called xšaθra vairya.
Ārmaiti appears with dominion, and humans seek her aid in acquiring it.
Vohu Manah precedes Šahrewar as his hierarchical superior in the divine order.
Vohu Manah appears jointly with dominion and helps make good rule effective.
Mithra receives the first of the three glories departing from Yima.
Astvat̰.ərəta possesses victorious Khvarenah and completes the frašō.kərəti.
Spənta Ārmaiti shares collectively in the Aməša Spəṇtas' possession of Khvarenah.
Spenta Mainyu sends Ātar to obtain the unseized Khvarenah.
Vohu Manah shares collectively in the Aməša Spəṇtas' possession of Khvarenah.
Yima possesses Khvarenah while his realm remains prosperous and free from affliction.
Divine Fortune dwells with Yima and sustains his extraordinary sovereignty.
Khvarenah abandons Yima in falcon form after his falsehood or deceit.

relations.myth: Jamšīd's pride and loss of farr
relations.note: Farr visibly leaves Jamšīd after he claims divine honor and sole credit for prosperity.

relations.myth: The lie and loss of Fortune
relations.note: Fortune abandons Yima in bird form after his deceptive word.
Mithra and Māh occur together in the same sacrificial catalogue.
Tištrya and Māh appear together in a ritual catalogue without a narrated encounter.
Māh is a later ritual fellow-worker of Wahman in caring for animals.
Māh is classified among Vohu Manah’s subordinate co-workers concerned with beneficial animals.
Rashnu accompanies Mithra's chariot, riding beside him on alternating sides.
Rashnu, Mithra, and Sraosha jointly pursue violators of covenants.
Mihr joins Rashn and Srosh in the judicial mediation of souls.
Rashn and Mihr join the yazads supporting Pēšyōtan.
Rašn weighs deeds while Mihr presides with him and Srōš at the tribunal.
A perjurer wards off Rashnu and deceives Mithra during the oath procedure.
Rashnu and Mithra are invoked together in formulaic liturgical pairings.
A rhetorical divine-family passage names Mithra and Rašnu as brothers.
A rhetorical divine-family passage calls Spənta Ārmaiti Mithra's mother.
Sraoša accompanies Mithra during his celestial movement.
Mithra drives enemy formations while Sraosha pursues them everywhere.
Mihr presides with Srōš and Rašn when the dead soul's deeds are judged.
Sraosha and Mithra sit with Rashnu in the soul’s judging tribunal.
relations.source: Dādestān ī Dēnīg 13; Mēnōg ī Xrad 2

relations.note: A rhetorical divine-family passage names Mithra and Sraoša as brothers.

relations.myth: Path opened for the arrow-like celestial flight
relations.note: Mithra opens or indicates the broad road for Tishtrya's arrow-like flight.
Vərəθraγna travels with Mithra and Rašnu to detect false oath-takers.
Protective recitation invokes Sraoša against decay, death, and Nasu’s corpse-pollution.
Spənta Ārmaiti is named as Rashnu's mother.
Rashnu, Sraosha, and Mithra jointly pursue covenant-breakers.
Srosh protects the soul and mediates at the bridge with Rashn and Mihr.
Rashn and Srosh join the yazads supporting Pēšyōtan.
Rashnu drives enemy formations another way while Sraosha pursues them.
Sraosha escorts the soul and sits beside Rashnu, who weighs its deeds.
relations.source: Dādestān ī Dēnīg 13; Mēnōg ī Xrad 2

relations.note: Sraosha is named as Rashnu's brother.
Good Wāy escorts the soul in the sequence where Rašn judges it.
Rashn and Wahrām join the yazads supporting Pēšyōtan.
Rašnu accompanies Vərəθraγna and Mithra in examining oath-breaking.
Wahrām assists the soul during its journey toward Rashnu's court.
Rašn and Wahman share duties connected with judgment and accounting.
Rashn appears beside Zamyād in later divine catalogues and blessing traditions.
relations.source: Greater Bundahišn; Āfrīn ī Haft Aməšaspand

relations.note: Spəṇta Ārmaiti joins the final rite and is freed from mountains and corruption.
Vohu Manah participates in Saoshyant’s final liturgy and defeats Aka Manah.

relations.myth: Distribution of the all-seed tree’s seeds
relations.note: Tištar rains seeds released by Sēnmurw and transported by Camrōš.
Sēnmurw appears within the council’s order of animals protected by Wahman.
Both participate structurally in Ahura Mazdā’s beneficent creation.

relations.myth: Cooperative operation of the divine powers
relations.note: Devotion operates with Spenta Mainyu, truth, Good Mind, and desirable dominion.
Ārmaiti increases dominion for those praised together with Vohu Manah.
Vohu Manah and Ārmaiti jointly participate in the Gāθic ethical constellation.
Yima invokes and presses Spenta Armaiti, who expands to accommodate creatures.
Ārmaiti is Earth's divine guardian or spiritual patron, but remains distinct from Zam.
Vayu reaches Spənta Mainyu’s creation, and worship addresses only his Spənta-associated aspect.
Vohu Manah defends Spenta Mainyu’s creation from Angra Mainyu’s invasion.
Vohu Manah advances alongside Spenta Mainyu in the contest for Glory.
Vohu Manah supports Spənta Mainyu’s beneficent side in the cosmic contest.
Good Mind accompanies or operates beside the beneficent spirit during revelation.
Spənta Mainyu sends three divine emissaries in the Fortune contest surrounding Yima.
Good Wāy cooperates with righteous Srōš in escorting the soul toward Chinvat.
Wahman and Srōš bring a ewe to suckle the endangered infant.
Sraosha is asked to come to the chosen person through Vohu Manah.
Wahman and Srōš share duties involving the accounting and judgment of souls.
Srōš instructs Jamshid how to make Ahriman turn and recover Tahmōraf.
Tištar summons Wahman as guide or intermediary so rain may fall.
Time shares formulaic cosmological company with Tištrya.

relations.myth: Invocation with Space and Infinite Time
relations.note: Vayu and Zurvan share long-dominion language and occur in a cosmic liturgical association.
Vohu Manah serves as the Beneficent Spirit’s emissary in Yima’s Fortune-cycle.
Zurvan joins Rām, firmament, Moon, and Gōš in assisting Wahman.

Adam.note: Manichaeism identifies Gēhmurd with Adam, the material first human containing imprisoned divine light.
Some Muslim chroniclers identify Gayomart directly with Adam.
One Islamic solution makes Gayomart a son of Adam rather than Adam himself.
Another Islamic genealogy makes Gayomart a later descendant of Adam.

Ahriman’s demons.note: Ohrmazd’s creations and Amahraspands oppose Ahriman’s demons throughout cosmic history.

Aka Manah.note: Later demonology pairs Aka Manah against Vohu Manah.
Aka Manah fights in the final battle accompanying Saoshyant’s work and is defeated by Vohu Manah.
Vohu Manah defeats his supernatural opposite Aka Manah.
Wahman’s beneficent presence prevents Akōman from entering or harming Zarathustra.

Akem Manah.note: Akem Manah joins the evil host opposing Atar and the good divinities.

Akō Manah.note: Akō Manah is an Evil Spirit emissary in the Fortune contest.

Akōman.note: Akōman serves as Ahriman's chief demonic intellect and agent of evil thought.

Amurdād.note: The dēw Zārič is systematically arranged as Amurdād’s opposing counterpart.

Amərətāt.note: Ahriman's forces attack Amurdad's plants, with Zairiz assigned as opponent.
Mazda associates Amərətāt with the promised reward of the righteous.
Amərətāt is one of the six canonical Amesha Spentas.
Amərətāt is named jointly with enduring dominion and the other divine powers.
Amərətāt shares collectively in the Aməša Spəṇtas' possession of Khvarenah.
Amərətāt participates in the final rite, defeats thirst, and realizes universal immortality.
Amərətāt and Ārmaiti appear together as members of the beneficent heptad.
Immortality accompanies Haurvatāt as a reward mediated through the beneficent spirit.
Amərətāt and Vohu Manah appear jointly within the beneficent divine order.
Later priestly classification places Zamyād among Amurdad's divine helpers.

Anagrān.note: Anagrān cooperates with Šahrewar’s metal within the ordered creation.

Angra Mainyu.note: Her worship formula repudiates Angra Mainyu, without depicting direct combat.
Vayu empowers Ahura Mazda to strike Angra Mainyu’s creatures and ranges through his creation.
Later theology directs Bahrām's victorious power against evil, without narrating a personal duel.

Apaosha.myth: White and black horses battle over rain
Apaosha.note: Apaosha first defeats Tishtrya, but the empowered Tishtrya wins their rematch.

Apōš.note: Ahriman sends Apōš against the rain-star Tištar.

Aramazd.note: Armenian tradition calls Anahit the daughter of Aramazd.
Anahit appears with Aramazd and Vahagn in Tiridates III's official devotion.

Armayel.note: Armayel secretly substitutes sheep brain and saves condemned youths.

Arnavāz.note: The Šāhnāma makes Arnavāz Jamshid’s sister.

Arštāt.note: Rashnu and Arštāt are repeatedly invoked together as juridical divine beings.
Aštād appears with Rashn and other yazads in judgment and funerary contexts.
Rashn and Aštād join the yazads supporting Pēšyōtan.

Arədvī Sūrā Anāhitā.note: She is named among Spandārmad’s helpers in guarding and purifying earth.

Arənavāčī.note: Dahāka holds her captive until Θraētaona liberates her.

Astwihād.note: Ahriman's death-demon Astwihād casts mortality upon the primordial human.
The death demon Astwihād is sent with diseases and demonic forces against Gayomart.

Astwihād.myth: Death produces the corpse polluted by Nas
Astwihād.note: Astwihād seizes mortal life; Nas pollutes the resulting corpse without directly encountering him.
Astwihād seeks the soul while Rashn conducts judgment at the bridge.
Sraosha protects the dead against the demon of death.
Astwihād.source: Later Avestan and Pahlavi funerary texts

Astłik.note: Their related cults shared the Ashtishat complex, without a surviving personal encounter.

Astō.vīδātu.note: Later books place this death-causing demon among the druzes associated with bodily corruption.

Astō.vīδōtu.note: Astō.vīδōtu binds the dying person, whom Vayu then leads away bound.
Middle Persian interpretation closely coordinates and sometimes effectively identifies Astwihād with Bad Wāy.

Aša.note: Sraosha shares Aša’s conceptual field and was later reinterpreted as righteous Srōš.

Aši.note: Anahita's description and royal-benefaction language borrow material associated with Aši.
Haoma worships Aši and requests the boon needed to capture Fraŋrasyan.
Aši is named as Rashnu's sibling.
Spenta Armaiti is named as Aši’s mother; Ahura Mazdā is her father.
Ašišwang is listed among Spandārmad’s helpers in protecting the earth.
Sraosha approaches accompanied by wealth-giving Aši.
Yima’s exceptional Fortune is recalled within Aši’s hymn.

Aši Vanguhi.note: Ahura Mazda is named as Aši’s father.

Aši Vaŋuhī.note: A rhetorical divine-family passage calls Mithra the brother of Aši.
Aši, the personified power of recompense, accompanies Mithra's progress.

Aši Vaŋuhī.myth: Good Reward follows the celestial arrow
Aši Vaŋuhī.note: Aši Vaŋuhī follows behind during the arrow-like journey associated with Tishtrya.

Aštād.note: Aštād is Amurdād’s helper, associated with truth, order, or salvation.
Aštād serves Amurdād in judgment and protection of plant-life.
Aštād protects Wīrāz in the bridge scene associated with Daena.

Aštād.myth: Khvarenah invoked in the Aštād Yašt
Aštād.note: Khvarenah appears liturgically within the hymn catalogued under Aštād.
Aštād and Mihr join the divine company aiding Pišōtan.
Aštād appears beside Zamyād in later divine catalogues and blessing traditions.
Aštād.source: Greater Bundahišn; Āfrīn ī Haft Aməšaspand

Až.note: Aša and Airyaman overcome Až during creation's final purification.

Bahrām.note: Bahrām and Ardībihišt jointly guard Ahriman in hell.

Barmāya.note: Zahhāk kills the marvelous cow that nourished the hidden Fereydun.

Batuʾāl.note: Some chronicles name Batuʾāl among Jamshid’s children.

Būiti.note: The Druj sent against Zarathustra is identified in the following phrase as Būiti.
Būiti is a Druj within the hostile demonic order and acts under Angra Mainyu’s command.

Būšyąstā.note: Sraosha’s cock defeats the sloth demon’s effort to keep humans asleep.

Camrōš.myth: Distribution of the all-seed tree’s seeds
Camrōš.note: Camrōš collects Sēnmurw’s released seeds and carries them into Tištar’s rain-cycle.

Chisti.note: Ashi and Good Chisti are invoked together without a narrated interaction.

Christ.note: Steiner presents Christ as the mediating balance between Ahrimanic and Luciferic extremes.

Dahmān Āfrīn.note: Apam Napat and Dahmān Āfrīn are invoked together without narrative interaction.

Dhyāni-Buddhas.note: Theosophical literature equated the Amesha Spentas with Dhyāni-Buddhas.

Dionysos.note: Some Sasanian silver may combine Anahita-like and Dionysiac imagery.

Drujaskān.note: Drujaskān belongs to Dahāg’s maternal genealogy.

Drvāspā.note: Haoma sacrifices to Drvāspā, who grants his requested power of capture.
Yima sacrifices to Drvāspā and requests power over creatures and demons.

Dužyāiryā.note: Tishtrya restrains the female pairikā Dužyāiryā with double and triple bonds.

Dāmōiš Upamana.note: Dāmōiš Upamana attends the prepared ordeal together with Rashnu.
Modern scholars identify Mithra's ferocious boar as Vərəθraγna or his manifestation.

Eblīs.note: Islamic-period Persian writing sometimes assimilates Ahriman rhetorically to Eblīs without making them historically identical.
Eblīs extracts obedience and persuades Zahhāk to murder his father.
Eblīs kisses Zahhāk’s shoulders, causing two living serpents to grow.
Disguised as a physician, Eblīs prescribes human brains for the serpents.

Elohim.note: Theosophical literature equated the Amesha Spentas with Elohim.

Erethe.note: Ashi and Erethe are coordinated in liturgical invocation.

Evil Vāy.note: Evil Vāy opposes the soul before Rashnu's judgment.

Father of Greatness.myth: Manichaean war of Light and Darkness
Father of Greatness.note: Ahrmēn belongs to the realm of Darkness opposing the Father of Greatness and Light.
Middle Persian Manichaeans use Zurvan as the Father of Greatness.

Fohat.myth: Theosophical cosmic fire in primordial waters
Fohat.note: Modern Theosophical teaching identifies Apam Napat with Fohat and cosmic electricity.

Fravashis of the righteous.note: Their aid prevents Druj from gaining power, rule, and embodied existence between earth and heaven.

Fravāk.note: Fravāk belongs to Dahāg’s extended paternal genealogy.

Frawāk.note: Pahlavi genealogical sequences place Frawāk among Gayomart's descendants.

Frazišt.note: Frazišt opposes the soul before it reaches Rashnu's judgment.

Fraŋrasyan.note: She refuses his request to seize the Iranian xᵛarənah in Vourukaša.
Fraŋrasyan dives three times for Khvarenah, but it escapes every attempt.

Future Saošyants.myth: Final removal of Angra Mainyu’s sovereignty
Future Saošyants.note: The future saviors use Airyaman’s formula to establish Ahura Mazdā’s final mastery.

Gad.note: Khvarenah was historically equated with the Aramaic and Semitic personification of fortune.

Gaokərəna.note: Gaokərəna is invoked with Ameretat and supplies nourishment contributing to immortality at renovation.

Garmayel.note: Garmayel secretly substitutes sheep brain and saves condemned youths.

Garshasp.note: Later genealogical traditions make Jamshid an ancestor of Garshasp.

Geuš Tašan.note: Geuš Tašan and Vohu Manah participate in the consultation over pastoral protection.

Geuš Urvan.note: Vohu Manah participates in the divine consultation concerning the Cow’s Soul.

Gnostic cosmocrators.note: Theosophical literature equated the Amesha Spentas with Gnostic cosmocrators.

Gomer.note: Some Islamic historians identify Gayomart with Gomer to place Persian origins after Noah.

Good Order.myth: Greek interpretation of Oromazes’ six gods
Good Order.note: Plutarch’s Good Order or Lawfulness is probably a Greek rendering of Xšaθra Vairya.

Good Vāy.note: Good Vāy assists the soul as it approaches Rashnu's court.

Great Nous.note: Manichaean Middle Iranian texts use Wahman terminology for the Great Nous.

Gāw ī ēwdād.note: Created opposite each other, Gayomart and the Ox suffer the Assault and become generative through death.

Gōš.note: Māh and Gōš are co-workers within Vohu Manah’s cattle-oriented divine group.
Gōš is a later ritual fellow-worker of Wahman in caring for animals.

Gōšurun.note: A late variant assigns Gōšurun the binding elsewhere performed by Haoma.

Gə̄uš Urvan.note: Vərəθraγna proclaims that rival ritualists deny the Bull's Soul proper worship.

Hadayānš.note: Saoshyant and his helpers sacrifice Hadayānš and mix its fat with white hōm.

Haosrava.note: Khvarenah grants Haosrava victory over hostile rulers and forces.

Haošyaŋha.note: She grants him sovereignty over daevas and hostile peoples.
Haošyaŋha possesses Khvarenah and rules successfully through its power.

Herakles.note: Antiochus I explicitly equates Artagnes with club-bearing, lion-skinned Herakles.

Homāyun.note: Some chronicles name Homāyun among Jamshid’s children.

Hōšang.note: Pahlavi genealogies place Hōšang later in the line descending from Gayomart.
Ferdowsi makes Hōšang Kayumars's grandson through Sīāmak.
Kayumars sends Hōšang to lead humans and animals against the demons.

Imra.note: Nuristani Imra is traditionally compared with Yama and Yima, though equivalence remains comparative.

Indar.note: Indar is one of Ahriman's principal archdemons, deployed against the Amahraspands.
Ardwahišt seizes or defeats Indar, who opposes righteous observance.

Iranian Glory.note: The Iranian Glory overcomes Aeshma and other hostile powers.

Jamag.note: Pahlavi tradition makes Jamag Jam’s twin sister.
Jamag exchanges clothes with a demon and unites with Jam.

Jeh.note: Jeh revives the stunned Ahriman by promising to injure the primordial man and bull.
Ahriman rewards or embraces Jeh; their kiss or gaze produces pollution in some recensions.
Jeh revives Ahriman and promises to afflict Gayomart and the good creation.

Jesus Christ.note: Manichaean Middle Persian texts use Aryāmān as a translation or interpretation of Christ.

Jesus the Splendor.note: Jesus the Splendor awakens Gēhmurd to his divine soul and imprisonment in matter.

Jesus the Splendour.note: Eastern Manichaean tradition reassigns the Iranian Moon name to Jesus in its light-ship cosmology.

Jāmāspa.note: He receives aid or knowledge from Anahita.

Karšipt.note: Karšipt attends Ohrmazd’s council beside Sēnmurw and elsewhere outranks it as chief of birds.

Karšipta.note: The marvelous bird Karšipta carries Ahura Mazdā’s religion into Yima’s enclosure.

Kavi Haosravah.note: She grants him sovereignty and victory over hostile riders.

Kavi Kavāta.note: Khvarenah adheres to Kavi Kavāta as founder of the Kayanian royal line.

Kavi Usa.note: She grants his request for rule over hostile beings.

Kayanian Glory.note: The Kayanian Glory attends the prepared ordeal together with Rashnu.

Kingly Glory.note: Spenta Mainyu’s party seeks the personified or quasi-personified Glory against the destructive party.

Kirsāsp.note: The preserved hero awakens and kills Dahāg after his final escape.

Kāvā.note: Kāvā denounces Zahhāk and mobilizes the people behind Fereydun.
Modern Kurdish tradition makes Kawa personally kill the tyrant Dehak.

Kərəsāni.note: Haoma casts down Kərəsāni for obstructing priestly teaching and movement.

Kərəsāspa.note: She grants his request to defeat the monster Gandarəβa.
The fravashis guard the hero Kərəsāspa’s body.
Kərəsāspa receives the third departing glory in a possibly secondary expansion.
Kərəsāspa becomes one beneficiary of Fortune after it leaves Yima.

Lakṣmī.note: Lakṣmī is documented as a contextual Indic comparison or syncretistic equation for Khvarenah.

Manaobago.note: The Kushan coin deity is plausibly but disputably identified with Vohu Manah.

Mani's five Light Elements.note: Manichaean translators applied Amahraspandān to ether, wind, light, water, and fire.

Manthra Spenta.note: Ahura Mazdā appeals first to Manthra Spenta, then commissions Airyaman to heal.

Mao.note: The Kushan lunar god Mao is a regional continuation or adaptation of Māh.

Mawrot.note: Armenian Mawrot is occasionally compared with Ameretat, but its transmission and relationship remain uncertain.

Mazda-created Radiance.note: The Mazda-created Radiance attends the prepared ordeal together with Rashnu.

Mašyā.note: Mašyā grows from Spandārmad-earth after she receives Gayōmard’s seed.

Mašyānag.note: Mašyānag grows from Spandārmad-earth after she receives Gayōmard’s seed.

Mašīa.myth: Birth of the first human couple
Mašīa.note: Mašīa develops from the intertwined plant grown from Gayomart's purified seed.

Mašīānag.myth: Birth of the first human couple
Mašīānag.note: Mašīānag develops from the intertwined plant grown from Gayomart's purified seed.

Merdās.note: Ferdowsi makes Zahhāk the son of the pious Arab king Merdās.

Mihr.note: Localized Armenian tradition places Mihr within Aramazd’s royal-divine family.
Mihr protects the bridge crossing within the expanded scene containing Daena.
Modern reconstruction proposes functional competition between Mihr and Vahagn, without a surviving combat narrative.

Miθra.note: Mihr and Wahman share functions in accounting deeds and judging souls.
Miθra receives a departure or portion of Fortune formerly possessed by Yima.

Murdiyānag.myth: Creation of the material first couple
Murdiyānag.note: Manichaean tradition pairs Gēhmurd as Adam with Murdiyānag as Eve.

Māraspand.note: Māraspand is listed among Spandārmad’s helpers in sustaining earth.

Māθra Spenta.note: Māθra Spenta is explicitly said to possess a fravashi.

Mąθra Spəṇta.note: Some classifications count the holy formula among Hordād’s helpers, though the assignment varies.

Mərəšāna.note: Worship of Hvar counters the hostile force Mərəšāna, whose interpretation remains uncertain.

Nairyō.saŋha.note: The divine herald visits Airyaman’s dwelling and delivers Ahura Mazdā’s healing request.
Nairyō.saŋha is classified as Asha’s helper.
Nairyō.saŋha is explicitly said to possess a fravashi.
Nairyō.saŋha accompanies Mithra during his divine progress.
Mihr and Nēryōsang join other divine powers in aiding the eschatological hero Pišōtan.
Nēryōsang keeps two seed portions while Spandārmad receives the remaining portion.

Narseh.note: Later genealogy lists Narseh among Jam’s brothers.

Nizišt.note: Nizišt opposes the soul before it reaches Rashnu's judgment.

Nåŋhaiθya.note: Later schemes pair Nåŋhaiθya or Tarōmāiti against Spəṇta Ārmaiti.

Nāŋhaiθ.note: Nāŋhaiθ is an Ahrimanic archdemon assigned against Spandarmad.

Nēryōsang.note: Nēryōsang carries Ohrmazd’s message to Ardwahišt before his intervention.
Nēryōsang receives and safeguards two purified portions of Gayomart's seed.
Nēryōsang and Rashn join the divine collective supporting Pēšyōtan.

Parendi.note: Ashi and Parendi are invoked together without a surviving joint narrative.
Parendi follows the arrow's journey on a light chariot beside Aši.

Parōdarš.note: Sraosha wakes his cock operative, who rouses worshippers and drives off sloth.

Parəndi.note: Parəndi, personified Plenty or Fullness, accompanies Mithra's chariot.

Pišōtan.note: Mihr joins an assembled divine company that aids the eschatological hero Pišōtan.

Prajāpatis.note: Theosophical literature equated the Amesha Spentas with Prajāpatis.

Primordial Bull.myth: Creation and death of the primordial bull
Primordial Bull.note: Ohrmazd creates the primordial bull, whose purified seed later generates beneficent animals.

Pēšyōtan.note: Rashn joins other yazads in supporting Pēšyōtan against religion's enemies.

Rasastat.note: Ashi and Rasastat are coordinated in liturgical invocation.

Rostam.note: Later genealogical traditions make Jamshid an ancestor of Rostam.

Rām.note: Māh and Rām are co-workers within Vohu Manah’s subordinate divine group.
Rām is a later ritual fellow-worker of Wahman in caring for animals.

Rāman.note: Rāman and Haoma are grouped as Vohu Manah's animal-protecting fellow-workers.
Middle Persian theology identifies Rām, giver of peace, with Good Wāy of long dominion.
Zurvan and Rāman receive the concluding liturgical invocation together.

Rātā.note: Good, far-seeing Rātā appears beside Spenta Armaiti in her liturgical invocation.

Saoka.note: Saoka appears beside Asha Vahishta and Airyaman in liturgical invocation.

Sarasvatī.note: Their proposed historical identity rests on disputed similarities in rivers, fertility, and knowledge.

Satavaesa.myth: Distribution of waters across the seven regions
Satavaesa.note: Satavaesa follows Tishtrya-raised waters and directs them toward the seven regions.

Saurva.note: Later demonology pairs Saurva's oppressive misrule against Xšaθra Vairya.

Saŋhavāčī.note: Dahāka holds her captive until Θraētaona liberates her.

Sephiroth.note: Theosophical literature equated the Amesha Spentas with the Sephiroth.

Shahrewar.note: The dēw Sāwul is systematically arranged as Shahrewar’s opposing counterpart.

Sleep.note: The radiant personification Sleep protects Gayomart temporarily by frustrating the demonic assault.

Snāvidhka.note: Snāvidhka threatens to abduct and yoke Spenta Mainyu, but Kərəsāspa kills him first.

Solomon.note: Medieval writers equate or conflate Jamshid with Solomon as demon-commanding wonder-kings.

Soul of the Cow.note: Aeshma participates in the violence and oppression afflicting the Cow.

Spenjagr.myth: Drought demons obstruct the primordial rain
Spenjagr.note: Spenjagr aids Apōš during Tishtrya's rain battle, though Tishtrya does not strike him.

Spitiiura.note: Spitiiura is explicitly called the Yima-cutter, though the act’s details are lost.
Later tradition makes Spitūr collaborate with Dahāg in cutting Jam apart.

Spityura.note: Spityura appears among the evil host opposing Atar, without individual combat.

Spitūr.note: Spitūr assists Dahāg in cutting Yima in two.
Later genealogy lists Spitūr among Jam’s brothers.

Srōš.note: Soroush brings the divine warning enabling Kayumars's house to act against the demons.

Suk.note: Māh receives cosmic happiness from the obscure being Suk.

Sāwul.note: Sāwul is an Ahrimanic archdemon assigned as Shahrewar's counterpart.

Sāwul.myth: Defeat of oppressive rule at renovation
Sāwul.note: Šahrewar seizes and defeats Sāwul, the demon embodying tyranny and bad rule.

Sīāmak.note: Pahlavi genealogies place Sīāmak later in the line descending from Gayomart.
Ferdowsi makes Sīāmak the immediate son of Kayumars.

Sōšāns.note: Airyaman guides or assists the final savior in accomplishing Frašō.kərəti.

Tahmōraf.note: Bundahišn and priestly traditions make Tahmōraf Yima’s brother.
Ferdowsi makes Tahmuras Jamshid’s father and predecessor.
Jamshid reaches into Ahriman and retrieves his swallowed brother’s corpse.

Tarōmaiti.note: The Airyaman Išya formula puts the daēvic power Tarōmaiti to flight.

Tarōmat.note: At the renovation Spandārmad overcomes the demon embodying contempt and perverse thought.

Tauriz.note: Tauriz is an Ahrimanic archdemon assigned against Hordad.

Tauru.note: Later demonology pairs Tauru's destruction, disease, or thirst against Haurvatāt.

Taurvi.note: Amurdād and Hordād jointly overcome Taurvi and Zairič at the renovation.

Taurwič.note: Taurwič is Haurvatat’s assigned demonic antagonist and is neutralized or destroyed at renovation.

Taxma Urupi.note: Taxma Urupi subdues and humiliates Ahriman by riding him as a horse for thirty years.
Ahriman becomes or is made into a horse for Taxma Urupi to ride.
In later tradition Ahriman extracts information about Tahmuras's fear through deception.
After discovering Tahmuras's fear, Ahriman throws and kills him.
Taxma Urupi possesses Khvarenah and overcomes destructive beings through it.

Tešub.note: Scholars connect Vahagn's fiery and dragon-reaping traits with Hurrian-Urartian Tešub.

The Aməša Spəntas.note: Worship of Hvar simultaneously counts as worship of the Aməša Spəntas.
Their throne occupies a celestial station above Hvar’s solar station.

The Waters.note: His name identifies him as the offspring or descendant of the divine Waters.
Boyce reconstructs the Waters called the Ahura’s wives as his wives.

Tigran.note: Tigran kills Aždahak, the legendary Armenian representation of Astyages.

Tiur.note: Anahit's temple stood near the temple of the oracular Tiur.

Tur.note: A Zabulistani princess bears Jamshid a son named Tur.

Tusa.note: She favors Tusa over the opposing Turanian sons of Vaēsaka.

Tāz.note: Tāz belongs to Dahāg’s extended paternal genealogy.

Tīr.note: Some Middle Persian passages equate Tīr with Tištar despite contradictory astronomical traditions.

Udāy.note: Udāy belongs to Dahāg’s maternal genealogy.

Urvatat-nara.note: Urvatat-nara is named the temporal authority within Yima’s life-preserving enclosure.

Ušēdar.note: He is Saoshyant’s elder half-brother through Zarathustra’s preserved seed.

Ušēdarmāh.note: He is Saoshyant’s elder half-brother through Zarathustra’s preserved seed.

Vahagn.note: Anahit, Aramazd, and Vahagn form the royal Armenian triad.
Their cults occupied the same sanctuary complex at Ashtishat.

Vanaintī Uparatāt.note: The hymn's framing dedication pairs Vərəθraγna with personified Conquering Superiority.

Vandarəmaini.note: Anahita refuses this hostile petitioner's request.

Victorious Winds.note: The Victorious Winds attend the prepared ordeal together with Rashnu.

Vistauru.note: He receives aid or knowledge from Anahita.

Vištāspa.note: Khvarenah supports Vištāspa in the establishment of Zarathustra's religion.

Vištāspa’s Fravashi.note: The venerated Fravashi of Vištāspa drives Druj from the realm of righteousness.

Vāta.note: Wind moves vapor and clouds after Tishtrya raises water from Vourukaša.

Vīfrō Navāza.note: She appears as a maiden, catches him after his flight, and restores him safely to earth.

Vīuuaŋᵛhant.note: Vīuuaŋᵛhant is Yima’s securely attested father.

Vīzarš.note: Vīzarš drags the wicked soul, opposing the protective escort tradition involving Good Wāy.

Vərəθraγna.note: Mazda identifies Vərəθraγna as a divine being made by Ahura.
Vərəθraγna is assigned as Asha’s calendrical helper.
The epithet victorious fire was secondarily reinterpreted as Fire of Bahrām, without an Avestan encounter.
Vərəθraγna.source: Middle Persian development of ātar vərəθraγan

Vərəθraγna.note: Vərəθraγna advances before Mithra as a metal-limbed boar and mangles covenant-breakers.
Vərəθraγna’s protective gift of xᵛarənah is compared to the great bird Saēna.

Wahrām.note: Wahrām protects the bridge crossing in the same vision involving Daena.
Wahrām assists the righteous soul’s passage alongside Sraosha.
Good Wāy, Srōš, and strong Wahrām jointly assist the soul’s journey.

Warahrān.note: Warahrān's fire safeguards Gayomart's cause because human seed is associated with fire.

Waran.note: Xēšm is closely associated with Waran in the demonic coalition.

Watery Xᵛarənah.myth: Distribution of rain among the lands
Watery Xᵛarənah.note: Watery Glory joins the divine beings distributing waters raised by Tishtrya.

White Hōm.note: White Hōm is Haoma's cosmic form or counterpart, though texts remain inconsistent.
White Hōm.source: Bundahišn; Dādestān ī Dēnīg; Pahlavi Rivāyat

Wizāreš.note: Wizāreš binds the wicked soul after Rashn detects its wickedness.

Wizārišn.note: Sraosha opposes Wizārišn when the demon attempts to bind the soul.

Wāta.note: Wād helps distribute Tištar’s water, indirectly nourishing and renewing Amurdād’s plants.

Wāta.myth: Seizing and raining the world's water
Wāta.note: Wāta assists Haurvatāt in seizing, distributing, and raining water.

Xrad.note: Xrad is listed as Spandārmad’s helper and an associated spiritual principle.

Xrūtāsp.note: The Pahlavi genealogy names Xrūtāsp as Dahāg’s father.

Xwarrah.note: Personified Glory joins Mihr and other divine beings in aiding Pišōtan.
Xwarrah and Rashn join the divine collective supporting Pēšyōtan.

Xšaθra Vairya.note: Ahrimanic rule and Sāwul oppose Shahrewar's good sovereignty and metallic creation.
Desirable dominion participates in the divine configuration through which immortality is granted.
Xšaθra Vairya is one of the six canonical Amesha Spentas.
Xšaθra appears with Haurvatat in Gathic petitions and later heptadic lists.
Xšaθra Vairya shares collectively in the Aməša Spəṇtas' possession of Khvarenah.
Xšaθra Vairya holds a ritual office and is associated with the metal’s melting.
Ārmaiti’s devotion complements and enables desired dominion in Gāθic theology.
Desirable dominion is realized through Spenta Mainyu and truth.
Vohu Manah and Xšaθra Vairya participate jointly in beneficent dominion.

Xᵛarənah.note: Ahriman seeks possession of the divine Glory and sends demonic allies after it.

Xᵛarənah.myth: Attempted seizure of the royal Glory
Xᵛarənah.note: Dahāka attempts to seize the mobile Glory, which escapes into Vourukaša.
Hvar’s shining enables the yazatas to gather and distribute Xᵛarənah.
Each manifestation of Vərəθraγna carries Mazda-created Glory.

Yama.note: Yima and Vedic Yama are cognate inherited figures, not an unchanged single deity.

Zairi.note: Later demonology pairs Zairi's hunger, poison, or decay against Amərətāt.

Zairika.myth: Demonic assault on water and vegetation
Zairika.note: Zairika opposes Amərətāt alongside Taurwič, confronting the paired Haurvatat–Amərətāt order.

Zairiz.note: Zairiz is an Ahrimanic archdemon assigned against Amurdad.

Zairič.note: Amurdād and Hordād defeat Zairič, Amurdād’s regular demonic opponent, at the renovation.

Zamyād.note: Zamyād serves Amurdād in judgment and protection of plant-life.

Zamyād.myth: Liturgical invocation with Kayanian and unseized Glory
Zamyād.note: Khvarenah is invoked alongside the earth-divinity and associated mountains.

Zarathustra.note: Ahriman offers Zarathustra worldly sovereignty if he abandons the Mazda-worshipping religion.
Ahriman unleashes demons, but Zarathustra defeats and disperses them through sacred formulas.
Ahriman and his demons flee in terror when the future prophet is born.

Zarathustra.myth: Demonic attacks on the infant prophet
Zarathustra.note: Ahriman's demons repeatedly attempt to kill the infant Zarathustra but fail.
Ahura Mazda tells Zarathustra to sacrifice to Arədvī Sūrā Anāhitā.
She appears as a maiden and teaches him her proper offerings and ritual qualifications.
Druj, identified as Būiti, attempts to kill Zarathustra but retreats before his prayer and glory.
Khvarenah supports Zarathustra's revelation, birth, and establishment of the Good Religion.
Zarathustra is named the spiritual authority within Yima’s life-preserving enclosure.

Zarathustra’s fravaši.note: Amurdād helps transmit Zarathustra’s bodily substance so it can unite with his pre-existent fravaši.

Zarathustra’s xwarrah.note: Amurdād helps transmit Zarathustra’s bodily substance so it can unite with his glory.

Zarathuštra.note: Zoroaster’s religious recitation neutralizes Dahāg’s magical constructions.

Zrēšom.note: Pahlavi genealogy makes Zrēšom a twin child of Jam and Jamag.

Zurwān.note: Time fixes Gayomart's survival at thirty years after the Assault.

pairikās.myth: Hostile aerial beings attack the water-stars
pairikās.note: Tishtrya drives the airborne pairikās away from the cosmic sea.

phoenix.note: Later traditions compare or conflate Simurgh with phoenix despite lacking its early rebirth cycle.

planetary spirits.note: Theosophical literature equated the Amesha Spentas with planetary spirits.

powers of Light.myth: Manichaean war of Light and Darkness
powers of Light.note: The power called Ahrmēn belongs to Darkness and opposes the Manichaean powers of Light.

primordial Bull.note: The primordial Bull is explicitly said to possess a fravashi.

roc.note: A manuscript illustration identifies the Simurgh with the originally distinct roc.

sons of Vaēsaka.myth: Opposing petitions of Tusa and Vaēsaka's sons
sons of Vaēsaka.note: She refuses the Turanian brothers' request and favors Tusa.

the Ahurānīs.note: The water-associated Ahurānīs are ritually described as wives of the Ahura.

the Aməša Spəntas.myth: Collective invocation of the divine heptad
the Aməša Spəntas.note: Xšaθra Vairya belongs to and is invoked with the collective divine heptad.
They hold Māh’s glory and distribute it over Mazda-created earth.

the Aməša Spəṇtas.note: The Aməša Spəṇtas collectively possess Khvarenah and perform beneficent acts through it.

the Bull or cattle of many species.myth: Joint veneration of Moon and cattle
the Bull or cattle of many species.note: Māh is worshipped jointly with the many-specied cattle originating through lunar purification.

the Glories.note: The Glories serve Amurdād in judgment and protection of plant-life.

the Kayanian Glory.note: The personified sacred Glory accompanies Saoshyant and his companions during renovation.

the demons.myth: Molten metal poured into the demons’ breach
the demons.note: Šahrewar pours molten metal into the breach through which the demons entered creation.
The demons oppose legitimate royal investiture and support false kingship.

the final savior.note: The final savior and helpers complete the renovation that renders Ahriman powerless.

the other Amesha Spentas.note: They remain silent, then repeat Ardwahišt’s recognition of Ohrmazd as creator.

the peacock.note: Ahriman creates or displays the peacock as evidence that he possesses creative ability.

the primordial bull.note: Ahriman's assault poisons or kills the primordial bull, whose death generates later life.

the six Aməša Spəntas.note: Plutarch reports that Oromazes created six beneficent gods.

the six Aməša Spəntas.myth: Material creation assigned among the Amahraspands
the six Aməša Spəntas.note: Ohrmazd creates the Amahraspands and assigns each a material creation.

the spiritual and earthly yazatas.note: They assemble when Hvar shines and distribute glory across the earth.

the thirty birds.note: Thirty surviving seekers behold themselves reflected as the Simurgh and lose their separate identities.

the three Glories.myth: Calendrical association of Earth and Glory
the three Glories.note: Zamyād and the Glories share later calendrical and priestly groupings without narrative interaction.

the uniquely created Bull.myth: Invocation of Moon and primordial Bull
the uniquely created Bull.note: Māh and the uniquely created Bull are jointly invoked in the Avestan hymn.

the uniquely created Bull.myth: Moon preserves the primordial Bull’s seed
the uniquely created Bull.note: Māh houses and purifies the dead primordial bovine’s generative seed.

the waters.myth: Worship of sustaining Earth and waters
the waters.note: Earth and the life-bearing waters are juxtaposed and worshipped in the same liturgy.

the yazads.note: The yazads join Ohrmazd’s host in defeating and annihilating the dēws.

the yazatas.note: The yazatas collectively possess Khvarenah and accomplish beneficent works through it.

Ābān.note: Ābān cooperates with Spandārmad concerning earth and water.

Ādur Wāzišt.myth: Lightning defeats Spenjagr during the rain battle
Ādur Wāzišt.note: Ādur Wāzišt strikes Spenjagr while Tishtrya combats the other rain-blocking forces.

Āpas.note: Haurvatat protects or embodies the perfected condition of the divine collective Waters.

Ārmaiti.myth: Opposition of false and right disposition
Ārmaiti.note: Druj-aligned beings oppose the right disposition embodied by Ārmaiti; no separate encounter survives.

Āsmān.note: Āsmān cooperates with Šahrewar’s material sphere, from which metal is derived.

Āspīgān.note: Pahlavi genealogy makes Āspīgān a twin child of Jam and Jamag.

Ātaxš.myth: Melting metals for the final river
Ātaxš.note: Fire melts the mountain metals belonging to Šahrewar for the final purification.

Āz.note: Xēšm is associated with Āz and serves as a demonic commander.
At the end, Āz swallows Xēšm and other demonic commanders.
Xēšm becomes Āz or Hyle's active destructive spirit.
Devouring greed acts as Ahriman's ally in Zoroastrian cosmology.
Manichaean fragments place Āz and Ahrmēn together among powers destined for imprisonment.
Airyaman and Ardwahišt descend to begin conquering the demon of destructive greed.
Ardwahišt and Airyaman descend to begin Āz’s conquest.
In Manichaean cosmology, Āz participates in producing Gēhmurd from matter containing stolen light.
Hordād and Amurdād, represented by water and plants, oppose Āz’s consuming appetite.
Sraosha strikes or defeats Greed during the final renovation.

Čamrūš.myth: Defense of Iran from invading peoples
Čamrūš.note: Borz awakens Čamrūš, which destroys the assembled invaders.

Čisti.note: Čisti, personified religious insight, accompanies or prepares Mithra's path.

Čistā.myth: Invocation of Insight and the Good Religion
Čistā.note: Daena and Čistā are jointly invoked and closely associated without being identified.

Śiva.note: Kushan Wesho combines a Vayu-related Iranian name with Śaiva form, bull, and attributes.

Śrī.note: Śrī is documented as a contextual Sanskrit translation or comparison for Khvarenah.
Khotanese Śśandrāmatā was used to translate Śrī in Buddhist eastern Iran.

Šahrnāz.note: The Šāhnāma makes Šahrnāz Jamshid’s sister.

Ǝrəxša.myth: Tishtrya's flight compared with the archer's arrow
Ǝrəxša.note: Tishtrya's swift celestial movement is compared to Ǝrəxša's supernaturally aided arrow.

ʿAnqāʾ.note: Arabic ʿAnqāʾ was progressively equated and fused with the Persian Simurgh.

Θraētaona.note: She grants victory over Aži Dahāka and possession of Saŋhavāc and Arənnavāc.
Θraētaona smites and defeats the three-headed Aži Dahāka.
Frēdōn strikes, binds, and imprisons Dahāg instead of killing him.
Θraētaona receives the second of the three glories departing from Yima.
Θraētaona becomes one beneficiary of Fortune after it leaves Yima.

Θwāša.note: Personified Time and firmament or space appear together in worship.
